surface_text: Leveler is one of the most important additives for super-conformal copper electroplating, which has been widely applied in the fabrication of nanoscale (or microscale) interconnect features in integrated circuits (ICs) and printed circuit boards (PCBs). Because the structure-property relationship of the leveler is not clear, the development of novel leveler with high microvia filling performance is very time-consuming and challenging. In this study, a series of triphenylmethane-based (TPM-based) molecules with different nitrogen-containing groups have been designed, synthesized, and investigated as novel levelers for superconformal copper electroplating. Their structure-property relationships are investigated by electrochemical analyses, contact angle measurements, and microvia filling electroplating experiments. It is found that the steric hindrance and the type of the nitrogen-containing groups (tertiary amine or quaternary ammonium with counter anions) in a leveler not only affect its adsorption ratio and strength on the copper interface, but also affect its adsorption preference on different copper crystalline plane. In combination with Cl−, polyethylene glycol (PEG, suppressor), and bis-(3-sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS, accelerator), all TPM-based levelers show excellent microvia filling performances in copper electroplating and their effective concentrations are related to their antagonistic ability against the accelerator SPS.

surface_text: According to the additives’ different electrochemical effects in the electroplating, the additives were categorized as accelerators, suppressors, and levelers, respectively. Bis-(3-sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS) [3,4] and its reduced monomer sodium 3-mercapto-1-propanesulfonate (MPS) [5,6] are most widely used accelerators. In electroplating, the accelerators can reduce the cathodic polarization and facilitate the copper reduction [7,8]. The suppressors are usually polyether compounds, such as polyethylene glycol (PEG) [9,10], polypropylene glycol (PPG) [11,12], or their copolymers [13,14]. In contrast to the accelerators, the suppressors synergistically work with chloride ions to increase the cathodic polarization and thus suppress the copper reduction. Leveler is another important additive used in the electrolyte to fulfill the super-conformal electroplating, which usually are nitrogencontaining molecules and positively charged in the acid electroplating solution. As reported, the levelers can adsorb at the highdensity charge region of the cathode to inhibit the copper deposition and level the copper surface [15]. In addition, the use of a leveler in the microvia filling electroplating solution can greatly expand the application concentration range of accelerators [16].

surface_text: This work investigated the influence of Sodium 3- (benzothiazole-2 -ylthio)- 1- propanesulfonate (ZPS) as a single additive on performance of copper foil. Electrochemical analysis indicates that ZPS is of accelerating effect during electroplating. Chronoamperometry and ex situ SEM confirm that Copper growth obeys 3D diffusioncontrolled instantaneous nucleation and growth process, with ZPS significantly increasing the density of active sites. A comprehensive theoretical framework combining density functional theory calculations, molecula dynamics simulations, and in situ infrared spectroscopy elucidates an adsorption-capturing acceleration mechanism: ZPS can adsorb on copper surface and “catch” free Cu<sup>2+</sup> to the active sites to accelerate the electrochemical reduction process coupled with adsorbed Cl<sup>−</sup> . Furthermore, a Turing oscillation growth model, supported by finite element simulations and AFM analysis, is proposed to describe the morphological evolution, wherein ZPS preferentially accumulates at valley regions, improving surface flatness through cyclic peak-valley transfer, though with inherently limited ultimate smoothing. Structurally, XRD shows ZPS promotes Cu (220) orientation, while HRTEM confirms the presence of twin boundaries, and lattice fringe measurements reveal a transition from (111)-dominated to (220)-dominated regions upon ZPS addition. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) further indicates grain refinement (mean size from 3.29 μm to 2.60 μm) and increased twin-boundary density, which contribute to strengthening via Hall-Petch and dislocation-blocking effects. In terms of performance, ZPS improves surface morphology and reduces roughness. Mechanical properties are optimized at 30 mg/L ZPS, with tensile strength reaching 331 MPa and elongation 3.78 %. Finite-element simulation of high frequency signal transmission demonstrates that the lowered roughness effectively mitigates the skin effect, reducing signal loss. Overall, this work provides a comprehensive mechanistic understanding of ZPS and dem onstrates its potential as a single additive for producing high-performance electrolytic copper foils.

Cyclic voltammetry and electrochemical impedance spectra indicate that ZPS is of accelerating effect during electroplating. surface_text: Blind hole copper electroplating is the primary technology used in the connectivity manufacturing process for printed circuit boards (PCB), semiconductor integrated circuit (IC) chips, and IC packaging substrates [1–3]. The issue of achieving complete filling of high-quality plated copper has become increasingly essential in light of the progress made in integrated and miniaturized electronic devices. This is particularly relevant as high-density interconnect printed circuit boards (PCBs) are transitioning towards through-hole and micro-hole designs with larger depth-to-diameter ratios [4]. In the process of copper plating on such PCB micro vias with a larger depth-to-diameter ratio, there is a very significant difference between a current’s density distribution inside and on the surface of the micro vias. In such an environment, the copper electrodeposition rate in the pore area will be significantly greater than that in the micropores’ bottom region, which will result in the coppe layer covering and sealing the pore area in a preferential manner, leading to internal defects in the pores. In order to achieve bottom-up superfilling of the micropores, a synergistic effect of different addi tives is required, namely accelerators, inhibitors, levelling agents and chloride ions. Accelerators are generally small molecule organic sul phides containing specific functional groups of (-S–S-), sulfhydryl (-SH) and sulphonic acid $\left( - S O _ { 3 ^ { - } } \right)$ groups, which typically preferentially adsorb at the micropore’s bottom and can hasten the electrodeposition of copper at the hole’s bottom. During copper electrodeposition, the inhibitor is usually adsorbed on the cathode surface and interacts with chloride ions to increase the overpotential, thereby achieving the inhibitory effect on the surface deposition of copper, Inhibitors are mainly macromolecular polyether or polyols [7]. The most prevalent inhibitors are polyethylene glycol (PEG), but in addition to PEG there are also polypropylene glycol (PPG) and triblock copolymers of PEG and PPG [8–10]. Levelling agents can be added in very small amounts compared to inhibitors to achieve a strong inhibiting effect and rapid deactivation, leaving the surface flat and smooth. Meantime, levelling agents also show an inhibiting effect o copper deposition but there is no substitute for inhibitors, which can be compared to short-acting inhibitors, while inhibitors show a moderate inhibiting effect and deactivate slowly, and throughout the plating process, the levelling agent gradually covers the copper surface, domi nating the completion of superconformal deposition [4,7]. surface_text: ABSTRACT: The copper connectivity technique is essential for achieving electrical interconnection in wafer level packaging (WLP), system in packaging (SiP), and 3D packaging. The essential processing material for copper connectivity is a copper sulfate electroplating solution in which organic additives play a crucial role in the regularity of copper electrodeposition. In this study, electrochemical tests, X-ray difraction, 3D profiling, and scanning electron microscopy were used to investigate the leveling efect and mechanism of polyquaternary ammonium urea-containing polymer (PUB2) in the process of copper electrodeposition on-chip copper connections. PUB2 has excellent polarization ability on the target surface, remains unafected by the sulfur additive SPS and poly(ethylene glycol), and displays a strong ability to regulate the copper deposition rate of through-holes and surface wiring. The waviness of the wafer surface wiring was reduced from 130 to approximately 70 nm after optimizing the PUB2 concentration, and the surface roughness was reduced from 10 to approximately 7 nm. The coating was dispersed evenly, and the rate of through-hole filling was improved by 57%. This study not only examined PUB2 leveling performance and mechanisms but also devised a research method and system for electroplating additives to facilitate the development and application of new electroplating additives.

Considering the complexity and broad variety of chip processes, there are diferences between the plating solutions used for diferent plating processes, plating machines, and semiconductor manufacturers. As a result, plating solutions are typically customized develop ment products. However, there are three main issues associated with the research on leveling agents both domestically and internationally. First, current research mostly uses theoretical calculations, electrochemical methods, and electroplating experiments to investigate the mechanisms and efects of electroplating additives. Unlike traditional electrodeposition, chip copper interconnection involves precise deposition in a narrow space or surface at the micronano level. The morphology and uniformity of the copper deposition layer have a direct impact on the electrical performance of the copper interconnection line, thereby influencing the overall chip performance.<sup>14,15</sup> Its characteristics mainly include small electroplating dimensions, dificulty in filling microholes with uneven current density, and high coating quality requirements. However, there is a distinct lack of comprehensive research on electroplating with structured wafers, which renders most research results unable to be applied in practice. Second, copper sulfate electroplating leveling agents are primarily composed of dye organic polymers such as JGB, which tend to generate significant pollution. With the development of wafer-level, system-level, and 3D packaging, the performance ofelectroplating additives is facing increased scrutiny and evaluation. As a result, the industry is urgently requiring the development of novel electroplating leveling agents. Third, the majority of the existing research is focused on developing independent research models for wafer surface wiring and through-hole filling. However, in practical IC manufacturing, through-hole filling and wiring are performed concurrently, which causes a gap between study findings and application.<sup>16−18</sup> Therefore, it is crucial to develop an application-based screening and evaluation strategy for electroplating additives.

surface_text: To meet the high-performance demands of current electronic devices, copper electroplating in blind vias must achieve flawless filling without cracks and gaps. This typically involves superfilling or botom-up filling techniques, where superfilling refers to a deposition process during electroplating in which the copper deposition rate at the botom of the blind vias is significantly higher than at the opening and surface, thereby achieving perfect filling of the vias [5]. To accomplish superfilling, an acidic copper sulfate system is com monly used in industrial applications. In this system, the choice of additives is crucial, primarily including accelerators, suppressors, and leveling agents. Accelerators, usually sulfur-containing organic compounds, adsorb on the electrode surface, refine the copper crystal structure, and promote copper nucleation. Their primary function is to combine with chloride ions to achieve depolarization, thus increasing the cathodic current density [6–9]. The most widely studied and used accelerators include SPS and MPS [10, 11]. Sup pressors, such as polyether polymers (e.g., PEG and PPG) [12–14], mainly inhibit the deposition of copper during electroplating by adsorbing on the surface of the plated parts and preventing the difusion of ${ \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ [15–17]. In systems containing both accelerators and suppressors, the role of leveling agents is indispensable. Leveling agents typically include certain nitrogencontaining organic compounds [18, 19], such as the dye-type leveling agents JGB [20], DB [18], ABPV [21, 22], and heterocyclic non-dye leveling agents such as 2-amino-4-methylbenzothiazole [23] (AMBT) and 2-mercaptopyridine [24, 25] (2-MP). Their main func tion is to work synergistically with suppressors to inhibit copper deposition on the surface of the plated parts, optimize current density distribution, enhance filling eficiency, and thereby prevent premature hole sealing that leads to voids [25–30]. Although the most efective leveling agents are often commercial secrets, high costs and poor environmental friendliness in the market make the development of new leveling agents both time-consuming and labor-intensive. Consequently, to date, only a few superfilling leveling agents have been specifically reported [31–33].

surface_text: Abstract: Levelers are indispensable additives for achieving void-free, bottom-up superconformal copper filling of microvias. Establishing the molecular-level correlation between leveler structure and performance is therefore essential to the continued advancement of microelectronic copper-plating technology. Herein, nitro blue tetrazolium chloride (NBT) is identified as an efficient leveler for copper microvia superfilling. A multiscale strategy—combining electrochemical measurements, X-ray photoelectron spec troscopy (XPS), density functional theory (DFT) calculations, and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations—is employed to elucidate the action mechanism of NBT and pinpoint its electroactive sites. Electrochemical tests show that NBT markedly suppresses copper deposition and, together with polyethylene glycol (PEG), effectively resists competitive ad sorption by bis-(3-sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS), thereby enhancing the microvia superfilling performance of the PEG–SPS–NBT additive system. DFT results reveal that the nitro groups and tetrazolium rings constitute the primary adsorption centers on the copper surface; the nitro groups additionally strengthen intermolecular interactions between NBT and PEG. MD simulations further confirm that NBT anchors onto the Cu(111) surface predominantly through these $\Nu { \cal O } _ { 2 }$ groups and the tetrazolium ring, while co-adsorbed PEG enhances the overall adsorption strength of NBT. The electroplating experiment demonstrates that NBT can act as an effective leveler for microvia superfilling. Moreover, XPS analyses further confirm the synergistic co-adsorption of NBT and PEG and verify that the $\Nu { \cal O } _ { 2 }$ groups and tetrazolium rings are the dominant adsorption sites of NBT. Collectively, the electroplating, XPS, electrochemical, DFT, and MD findings clarify the structure–activity relationship of NBT and provide rational guidelines for designing next-generation copper-plating levelers.

surface_text: As is well known, nitro blue tetrazolium chloride (NBT), a commercially available tetrazolium dye, has demonstrated excellent performance as a leveler in through-hole copper filling [28–30]. In contrast, blind microvias present a far more challenging environment: with only one opening, electrolyte circulation is severely restricted, the diffusion layer thickens, and a pronounced ohmic and activation overpotential gradient develops. These factors make void-free filling in blind microvias significantly more difficult than in through-holes. To date, however, the suitability of NBT for blind-microvia superfilling has not been reported, nor has its structure–performance relationship been elucidated—an omission that limits the molecular-level insight into tetrazolium-based levelers and the rational design of cost-effective additives. Accordingly, NBT was chosen as the leveler in this study to assess its effectiveness in copper superfilling of microvias, of which the molecular structure is shown in Figure 1. By combining electrochemical analyses, electroplating experiments, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), MD simulations, and DFT calculations, we elucidate how NBT’s NO<sub>2</sub> groups and tetrazolium ring govern the adsorption on Cu(111) and synergism with PEG and other species. The insights provide rational guidelines for engineering the next-generation, robust, and economical levelers.

surface_text: In advanced electronic manufacturing, additives play a pivotal role in achieving high-quality metal interconnect by enabling precise pattern filling during electrodeposition. Currently, due to complex mechanisms, vast molecular spaces and lack of predictive models, the development of additives still relies on inefficient trial-and-error methods. Bayesian optimization is employed to optimize model accuracy by tuning hyperparameters, and SHAP analysis provides interpretable chemical insights. Three novel additives are identified, which are 2-aminopyrazine (APZ), 1-methylimidazole-4,5-dicarbonitrile (MIDCN), and 2-amino-4-ethylpyridine (AEP). Furthermore, superconformal filling of through‑silicon vias (TSVs) with aspect ratios >5 is achieved. The identified additives provide new insights into industrial metalli zation solutions for scaled-down nodes.

surface_text: In recent years, many studies have focused on the development of additives for cobalt superconformal electrodeposition and the underlying superfilling mechanisms [11–16]. Consequently, in the electrodeposition field, ΔE has been considered as a practical criterion for identifying promising additives [20], as molecules with smaller ΔE values generally exhibit stronger adsorption affinity toward the metal surface and thus exert more significant regulatory effects on the electrodeposition process [21–24]. An et al. [25] demonstrated a strong correlation between ΔE and both calculated adsorption energies and electrochemically measured inhibition ability, successfully applying this metric to identify Methylene Blue as a promising candidate for Cu electroplating.

Specifically, the purple region clearly illustrates the distribution of Co, while the yellow region serves as a structural reference, corresponding to the elemental mapping of the silicon substrate. This consistent and homogeneous distribution of Co demonstrates the effectiveness of these candidates as additives in achieving uniform and void-free Co deposition in high-aspect-ratio microstructures. The underlying bottom-up filling mechanism can be described as follows (Fig. 8b). In the initial stage of electrodeposition, additives uniformly adsorb onto the cobalt surface. As the deposition proceeds, the additive molecules within the TSV trenches are gradually depleted. Owing to mass transport constraints, the replenishment of additives inside the deep vias occurs at a slower rate than on the upper surface, resulting in a reduced inhibitor concentration within the trenches compared to the via opening. This concentration gradient leads to weaker suppression at the bottom of the via relative to its top. Consequently, the deposition rate is elevated at the bottom in comparison to the top, facilitating bottom-up filling and thereby enabling the formation of void-free interconnect structures.

surface_text: Conventional damascene electroplating utilizes a combination of organic additives, namely, a suppressor, an accelerator, and a leveler, to achieve superconformal fill of interconnects. In the DCEF mechanism, the presence of a sacrificial oxidant, such as H<sup>+</sup>, O<sub>2</sub>, or an organic additive, promotes a difference in metal deposition rate between the field and the feature bottom. Addition of a single suppressor-type additive assists in driving the plating rate differential. By appropriately selecting the sacrificial oxidants, organic additives, the waveform, and the mass transport conditions, void-free superconformal cobalt fill can be achieved in a variety of features.

surface_text: Thin film deposition technology is critical to realize high-quality cobalt interconnects. Physical vapor deposition [12,13] (PVD), chemical vapor deposition [14,15] (CVD), atomic layer deposition [16–18] (ALD), and electrodeposition [19–21] are the primary synthesis methods reported to date. PVD is a widely used film deposition technique, yet its filling efficiency and step coverage remain inadequate, primarily due to one-direction linear de position characteristics. This results in particles with large incidence angles failing to enter the trenches and instead depositing at the trench openings [22]. Consequently, the opening closes before the trench is fully filled [23]. To solve this problem, the industrial sector has de veloped specific PVD technologies, such as ionized PVD and collimated sputtering [24,25]. Nevertheless, the hole problem in small-sized channels still exists. In addition, CVD tech nologies have better filling capabilities, especially when trench widths are around several hundred nanometers, such as plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition [26]. ALD possesses the unique characteristic of layer-by-layer self-limiting growth, providing exceptional step coverage and film uniformity. However, its deposition rate is exceedingly low, making it particularly suitable for applications such as barrier layers and seed layers [27]. In contrast, electroplating technology is extensively utilized in damascene copper interconnect processes, where it enables bottom-up film growth and demonstrates remarkable filling capabilities [28,29]. During the electroplating process, precise control over parameters such as applied current, anode material, accelerants, inhibitors, planarization agents, and mass transport allows for the fine-tuning of deposition rate, grain size, morphology, impurity content, and stress [30]. This level of control highlights the considerable potential for further advancement of metal-interconnect trench-filling techniques.

surface_text: Cobalt electroplating is an efficient and cost-effective method for achieving highquality cobalt interconnects [31,32]. By introducing certain organic additives into the plating solution, bottom-up cobalt superfilling can be realized. Superfilling refers to the phenomenon where the metal deposition rate at the bottom of a trench exceeds that in the side wall. This technique is particularly crucial for the fabrication of interconnects with high aspect ratios, as it effectively prevents the formation of voids, ensuring the integrity and reliability of the interconnects. To date, multiple super-conformal filling mechanisms have been proposed by different research groups. The S-shaped negative differential resistance [33,34] has been extensively applied to the overfilling processes of various metals, including copper [35], gold [36], nickel [37], cobalt [38], and zinc [39]. This model suggests that the adsorption and desorption behavior of inhibitors on the electrode surface leads to a nonlinear variation in current density within a specific potential range, resulting in an “S”-shaped curve. By optimizing inhibitor concentration and potential control, this model enables the realization of the bottom-up overfilling of metals in high-aspect-ratio structures. Rigsby et al. [40,41] introduced the differential current efficiency fill mechanism, emphasizing the critical role of the H<sup>+</sup> concentration gradient in overfilling processes. They observed that during the electrodeposition of cobalt, the pH gradient rapidly formed within the trenches due to proton transfer, resulting in a disparity between the current efficiency and deposition rate at the trench interior and the opening. This differential effect facilitated the bottom-up filling of cobalt. In parallel, Wu et al. [42] introduced the hydrogen reduction-induced deactivation mechanism, which elaborates on how changes in pH and H<sup>+</sup> concentration affect the inhibitory efficacy of additives, thereby triggering a bottom-up filling mechanism. That model showed that the self-initiated bottom-up filling of cobalt was driven by the reduction in and deactivation of inhibitors at the bottom of the trench, caused by hydrogen gas evolution, leading to a diminished inhibitory effect and subsequently promoting the deposition rate at the bottom. The adsorption energy determines the conformality of deposited cobalt layers, especially in complex geometries structures, but its role in achieving superconformal filling has been largely overlooked. Addressing this gap is essential for improving the precision and reliability of coating processes in advanced applications.

surface_text: With the continuous development of chips towards high integration, the chip interconnect size is constantly decreasing and copper interconnect technology faces huge challenges. When the interconnect size is reduced to below 7 nm, copper wire conducts exponential growth in resistivity due to its grain boundary scattering [1, 2], leading to chip overheating and increased power consumption, which in turn affects the computing speed and overall device performance [3]. On the other hand, copper interconnects require a barrier layer of approximately 2 nm tantalum nitride (TaN) to prevent copper metal from diffusing into the silicon dielectric layer, thus further increasing the interconnect resistance [4]. Metal cobalt has the advantages of short electron mean free path, resistance to electromigration and good compatibility with semiconductor manufacturing, which has been considered as a new type of interconnect material to replace copper [5–7]. Currently, the pioneer manufacturers such as Intel and TSMC are also proposing to adopt cobalt as a new interconnect metal for advanced chip manufacturing [8]. At present, the cobalt interconnects in silicon chip are realized through electroplating cobalt super-filling. Although there have been reports on the research of electroplated cobalt super-filling in chip microholes [9–11], compared with electrodeposited copper, electrodeposited cobalt is prone to forming holes and cracks due to such issues as hydrogen evolution, homogenization and poor coating quality [12]. Electroless plating is one of the most practical routs to realize cobalt plating in industrial-scale since it presents a good coverage ability, facile processing and low cost. Particularly, additives play a crucial role in electroless plating [13–16]. The appropriate additives not only can improve the quality of the chemical coating, but also enhance its properties such as density, corrosion resistance, wear resistance, and conductivity.
